# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 4 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_004_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 1, Chapter 4

**1** Brothers and sisters, I received a vision twenty days after the former one — a prefiguring of the tribulation that is coming. **2** I was walking on a country road about ten stades from the main road, in terrain that is very difficult to traverse. **3** As I walked alone, I asked the Lord to complete all the revelations and visions he had shown me through his holy church — to strengthen me and grant repentance to all his servants who had gone astray — so that his great and glorious name might be glorified, since he had thought me worthy to show me his wonders. **4** While I was glorifying him and giving thanks, something like a voice replied to me: "Do not be double-minded, Hermas." I began to reason within myself, "How can I be double-minded, after the Lord has established me and I have seen such glorious things?" **5** A little further on, brothers and sisters — behold, I saw dust rising as if reaching toward the heavens, and I said to myself, "Is a herd of cattle coming, stirring up dust?" But it was about a stade away from me. **6** As the dust rose higher and higher, I began to suspect it was something divine. The sun came out briefly, and behold I saw before me a great beast like an enormous sea-monster, with fiery locusts pouring from its mouth. The beast was about a hundred feet in height and its head was like a large jar of earthenware. **7** I began to weep and to pray to the Lord to rescue me from it. Then I recalled the word I had heard: "Do not be double-minded, Hermas." **8** So then, brothers and sisters — clothed in faith in the Lord, and calling to mind the great and glorious things he had shown me — I took courage and faced the beast. The beast was coming with such rush and force that it could have destroyed an entire city. **9** I drew close to it, and the great beast stretched itself flat on the ground and did nothing but put out its tongue; it did not move at all until I had passed it by. **10** Now the beast had four colors on its head: first black, then fiery and blood-red, then golden, then white.

---

### Council Notes

This chapter is Vision 4 in traditional numbering but is placed here as part of the continuous vision sequence. The great beast is the apocalyptic tribulation personified — a classic Jewish-Christian apocalyptic image (cf. Daniel 7, Revelation 13).

The four colors on the beast's head (v. 10) are interpreted by the elderly woman in the next chapter: black = the world, blood-red = destruction, gold = the chosen who escape, white = the coming age. This is explicit typological allegory.

The instruction "do not be double-minded" (me dipsycheis) is a key Hermaic concept — the opposite of single-hearted faith. It recurs throughout the Mandates.

Hermas passing the beast unharmed by faith alone is the central dramatic image of the Visions.
